newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Hungary, Romania boost ties, eye NATO admission.
newsitem.headline: Hungary, Romania boost ties, eye NATO admission.

text.p: The defence ministers of Romania and Hungary on Monday hailed the growth of ties between the two countries and vowed to link efforts to attain their goal of early admission to NATO.
"We reiterated mutual support for our individual bids to join NATO," Romanian Defence Minister Victor Babiuc told a news conference shared with his Hungarian counterpart Gyorgy Keleti.

Bucharest is lobbying hard to be invited -- alongside more advanced East Europeans Hungary, Poland and the Czech Republic -- when the Atlantic Alliance announces its first eastward expansion at a Madrid summit in July.

Romania is still seen as a longshot for early admission, despite recent praise from the West, especially since it signed a key treaty with Hungary last year, patching old rifts over borders and ethnic minorities.

But ties between Budapest and Bucharest -- long strained by disputes over the status of Romania's 1.6 million ethnic Hungarians -- would not sour should either country fail to win early NATO membership, Keleti said.

"Should one of our two countries, Hungary or Romania, be left out of first-wave enlargement, we should continue to boost our relations in order to prove that the country that was left out is mature and fit for NATO membership."
Romania and Hungary will foster their strategic partnership and create a joint peacekeeping unit by the end 1997 with Franco-German support, the two ministers said.

Babiuc, who took over the top defence job after the centrists' election win over ex-communists last November, said Romania would not change from its pro-NATO option, whether or not it fulfils its early admission goal.
"We do want to join together (with Hungary), but we can't afford to ignore a different possibility."
Failure to be among first entrants would have a backlash on public opinion, he said."There will be frustration, but I don't think that could lead to instability (in Romania)."
Keleti praised NATO's attempts to sign a pact with Russia to allay Moscow's concerns over the expansion of North Atlantic Treaty Organisation to take in former Soviet-bloc countries.

"The present Russia-NATO negotiations are a recognition of Russia's status as a power in this region," he said. "But we cannot accept that Russia should have a right of veto over a sovereign country's admission, such as Hungary's."
